maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1965-66 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1966, was presented by Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1965-66 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house, in view of the important nature of these estimates and because I understand there are a number of matters to be raised before we reach motions, I should like to make a short statement to the house. I suggest that this might be done on the understanding that opposition spokesmen be also free to make their usual statements at this time.
The budgetary expenditures provided for in the estimates for the coming fiscal year commencing April 1, 1965, including amounts already authorized by continuing statutes as well as moneys parliament is being requested to appropriate, amount to $7,399,727,432. Parliament is also being asked to authorize the disbursement of moneys for loans, investments and advances, which add to the government's active assets, in a total amount of $202,144,800.
Not included in these totals, but set out in the estimates for information, is the forecast amount for old age security pension payments amounting to $905 million. These pension payments are separated from the budget figures and are payable out of the old age security fund to which are credited the taxes levied for this particular purpose. The figure shown in the blue book does not include the increased payments contemplated by the Canada pension plan legislation.
To compare the main estimates for 196566 with the total expenditures authorized by parliament to date for the current fiscal year would, of course, be misleading. The new year's estimates take no account of the supplementary requirements which parliament will be asked to approve in the course of the year. It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that a reasonably accurate comparison of total expenditures for the year commencing April 1, 1965 with those for the current and previous fiscal years must await the budget presentation.
It is also misleading to compare the main
estimates for the coming fiscal year with the main estimates for the current year. For example, the subsidies and special compensation payments to the provinces which are statutory are shown in 1965-66 at some $127 million more than the amount included in the main estimates for 1964-65. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the increase in these payments in 1965-66 over the expected actual expenditures in 1964-65 is only $38 million because of increases during the current year consequent upon new federal-provincial arrangements entered into following the preparation of last year's blue book.
There is also the fact that the programs envisaged by the Atlantic Development Board Act are shown for the first time in the 196566 blue book, whereas expenditures are being incurred during 1964-65 by virtue of the appropriation granted by that act.
On the other hand, the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce register a decrease of about $19 million from 1964-65. The bulk of that amount represents the balance of the federal payment to the Canadian corporation for the 1967 world exhibition which, when paid during the current year, will not be repeated in the new year.
Changes in statutory expenditures between years result in an over-all increase of $343.6 million. Beyond the $127 million increase shown for subsidies and special compensation to the provinces-and I would repeat that the actual increase is $38 million-and the new $25 million item for the Atlantic development board program, both mentioned earlier, the principal increases are: $64 million in payments to provinces under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act; $63.2 million in interest and other charges related to the public debt; $55 million in forgiveness of indebtedness by the municipal development and loan board, and

Main Estimates
$46.5 million for youth allowances payments, a new item.
An increase of about 1.5 per cent will be noted in the provision for the Department of National Defence, reflecting increasing costs generally and initial provision for the five year defence equipment program announced recently, offset somewhat by the savings being achieved by departmental reorganization. For 1965-66, funding for the armed forces is being combined in one vote to facilitate the adjustments necessary for integration of the forces, but the same degree of information is provided in the details of estimates as for other years.
When I tabled the main estimates a year ago I indicated that a special program review had been instituted during the summer months of 1963 as a prelude to the customary treasury board review of departmental proposals in the fall of the year, and that substantial cut-backs in many expenditure programs were achieved as a result of that examination. That procedure was refined and extended last summer. Its effectiveness and usefulness was such that it is intended to make it a permanent feature of the government's annual budgetary procedures.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the house to changes in the form of the estimates for 1965-66. The unemployment insurance commission has hitherto had its estimates listed in the blue book with those of the Department of Labour. In the 1965-66 blue book the unemployment insurance commission's estimates are shown in a separate section located, alphabetically, immediately after the estimates of the Department of Transport and immediately before the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Other services have been transferred to new locations in the blue book as a result of transfers under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. They
are: the Atlantic development board transferred from Secretary of State to the Minister of Transport; the centennial commission and the economic council of Canada both transferred from Privy Council to the Secretary of State, and the national museum of Canada, which has been transferred from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to the Secretary of State.
Another change, one which puts into effect a proposal which was made to the government by the standing committee on public accounts, is the inclusion of a new appendix to the blue book, commencing on page 525, entitled "Public Service Employment". This appendix comprises an over-all summary of establishment and staff strength statistics for all the federal departments and agencies for which financial provision is contained in the earlier sections of the blue book.
With the permission of the house I now propose to table for inclusion in Hansard three tables relating to the 1965-66 estimates. The first table compares the 1965-66 estimates with the total budgetary estimates for several preceding years. The second table compares statutory expenditures for 1965-66 with those for
1964-	65. The third table indicates the changes in the main estimates between 1964-65 and
1965-	66 by an examination of operating, capital and other costs.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize again that the main estimates which I have tabled in the house today do not provide any reasonable comparison of total expenditures for next year with those of the current or previous fiscal years. That comparison must await the budget presentation.

Hon. George C. Nowlan (Digby-Annapolis-
Kings): Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have listened with a high degree of interest to the involved and highly technical statement just made to the house by the Minister of Finance. I do not propose, of course, to discuss it in any detail this afternoon. It is always inadvisable to do so at any time before one has had a chance to consider the figures; and particularly in view of the fact that the minister has told us this afternoon that there is no basis of comparison between these estimates now being tabled and the estimates which have heretofore been tabled it certainly would be a waste of time for me to indulge in any attempt at comparison. I quite appreciate the fact that there have been changes in the format and presentation, and there are many other matters which enter into the picture.
I am particularly intrigued, however, by the fact that the minister says there can be no comparison made until after he brings down his budget. I presume this implies a very early presentation of the budget to the House of Commons, and it is obvious from this that the minister is expecting to produce the budget improving his financial position a great deal in the near future. I am confident that he can, because the prosperity of which we hear so much is based on policies established by the prior government.
I am not going to discuss the details further at the moment. As the minister says, they can be discussed much better when the budget has been brought down and when we have had a chance to compare the very involved figures representing the total estimates for the next fiscal year and those of former years.
I am also somewhat intrigued by one matter. I am not sure what the minister's intention is. Ordinarily when the minister brings in his estimates he moves, after all statements have been made, that the estimates be referred to the committee of supply. Whether he intends to do that this afternoon I am not sure, and quite frankly I have not checked the rules to see what the situation is. However, I am sure it is the great hope of the house that in the very near future this session will be prorogued and a new session started. I would expect that the life tenure of the committee of supply might be in question if prorogation should take place. It may be that simply as a matter of courtesy the minister is supplying the house with the estimates this afternoon for us to consider prior to his moving to refer them to the committee of supply in the subsequent session.

On the other hand, if he intends to move-such a motion this afternoon I should like to-reserve my position as to the legality of such a procedure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that now is not the time to try to make any exhaustive comment on the minister's presentation this afternoon. We shall have an opportunity to do that later when he brings down his budget, and I might say that the house always awaits the budget of the Minister of Finance with great interest, shall I say, and perhaps a certain anticipation.
There is one thing for which I have looked and have not been able to find, but I was hoping I would be able to find some indication of a substantial increase in our efforts toward world development in the way of the advance of credits and grants to the developing countries. I have in mind the fact that Canada supported the United Nations resolution for the devotion of 1 per cent of our gross national product, an amount agreed upon by most developed countries, to be paid toward development in other countries. This would entail an item of some $430 million. No one knows at the moment whether we will achieve that objective. I hope that somewhere in the minister's calculations there has been a provision for a very substantial increase in Canada's contribution toward world development and, by that means, toward world peace.

maintopic: TABLE III
speechtext:
As has
been pointed out, it would be difficult, if not impossible and perhaps undesirable, to comment on the details of the estimates that have just been tabled by the Minister of Finance. We note, however, that there are another $7 billion of estimated expenditures with which this house is going to deal during the next session of this parliament, which may begin soon as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings suggested. However, if we look at some of the legislation still to come before us and some of the other points of contention, it may not be as soon as the President of the Privy Council would hope.
We in this party, Mr. Speaker, are alarmed at the increase again of an estimated $62 million in interest charges on the national debt. This is something that goes on year after year which we, at least, cannot accept as an inevitable thing. We think something could and should be done about it. Nevertheless this item appears every time the blue book is presented to this parliament; there

is a large and significant increase in these debt service charges, particularly the aggregate amount of interest that is paid on the national debt.
We believe that the appendix which gives some details of the establishment respecting staffs and so on is a very useful addition to this blue book, because it will give us an opportunity to make some comparisons from year to year in over-all employment in the public service.
The last words of the minister's statement this afternoon were to this effect: "I should like to emphasize again that the main estimates which I have tabled in the house today do not provide any reasonable comparison of total expenditures for next year with those of the current year or previous fiscal years." I remember, Mr. Speaker, that not so long ago we had a rather interesting debate on this particular matter between the Minister of Finance, the previous minister of finance the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, and other members. There seemed to be some deliberate attempt by the Department of Finance to mislead the house. I am not suggesting that this was an acknowledged thing, that they did not put in accurate figures with respect to the debt service charges, but it was suggested if the situation were otherwise it would be possible for some people familiar with these things to anticipate what was going to be in the next budget.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that we would reach a point some time when the estimated expenditures as the Department of Finance can calculate them will be closer to the actual number of dollars spent, rather than have parliament faced with this statement year after year that we cannot use these estimates as a basis for any reasonable comparison.
Now, this is perhaps not a deliberate way of trying to deceive the house, but it seems to me there are no qualms about putting in figures that will not give the house an opportunity of making a valid or reasonable comparison. Somehow, Mr. Speaker, I think we should try to get around this problem.
In conclusion, I hope the House of Commons can find some way of dealing with the 24 departments and $7 billion so we will not find ourselves spending about 80 days in committee of supply passing the details of this expenditure through the house. To a greater or lesser degree all hon. members specialize in certain departments. There has been a great deal of criticism of the house when it is in committee of supply due to the fact that there are from only 30 to 40 and some-
Main Estimates
times up to 60 members present when the estimates of a particular department are being considered, with all the other members, who specialize or are interested in other departments, waiting for that particular department's estimates to pass.
It seems to me we need to devise some other way so that members can be looking into more than one department at the same time. The fifteenth report of the special committee on procedure and organization made some suggestions in that regard, and I hope action can be taken on it fairly soon.

Mr. Speaker, in a matter of a few minutes the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has announced that the government would spend the tidy sum of $7,400 million next year. It only took him about six or seven minutes to announce that the government would be spending that amount.
To be able to announce, just like that, such astronomical expenditures must make the Minister of Finance feel quite important.
However, in listening to the Minister of Finance I could not help but think that in the final analysis that amount would be coming from the Canadian taxpayers' pockets. Canadian citizens throughout the country will be paying taxes for a whole year in order to ensure that the federal government treasury can afford to spend the $7,399 million referred to.

maintopic: TABLE III
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: TABLE III
speechtext:
In other words, the Minister of Finance announced that such expenditures would be made, but it would be proper to announce that the Canadian citizen will have to pay taxes and that the money thus collected will be derived from his labour, his sweat, his profits, his interests.
As pointed out a moment ago, the greatest increase forecast will be in the interests to be paid on the national debt: $1,101 million next year. This is twice as much as family allowances to be paid out across the country; it is more than what will be spent on unemployment assistance and more than what will be spent for the hospital insurance or the pension plans.
As a matter of fact, when I look at the vote respecting unemployment assistance, on page 225 of the report, I find that last year $115 million have been spent in this respect while the same amount is earmarked for this year.

Main Estimates
As far as the debt is concerned, interest charges have increased by $63 million, which is equivalent, by itself, to 50 per cent of the forecast expenditure for unemployment insurance.
In looking at the items in respect of old age assistance, and assistance to the blind and the disabled, I find an increase of only one and a half millions, whereas with respect to the debt service charges, there is an increase of the order of $63 million.
Therefore, where is the Canadian government going in 1965?
I appreciate that the Minister of Finance prefers to talk with those around him instead of listening to the truths now being pointed out to him; but why could he not try, with the help of competent officials, to modernize the method of preparing the budget which is established according to procedures dating back to 1910? As a matter of fact, the budget is still being prepared as it was in 1900. Why could the Minister of Finance not introduce in the future a budget taking into account every Canadian citizen instead of the financiers? At present one seventh, that is, for every dollar spent, from 15 to 18 cents will be paid in interest to high finance and increase our national debt.
It is another Liberal budget favouring capitalists, chartered banks, financiers and not a budget in favour of the Canadian people, of workers, of the unemployed and of farmers in general.
What is done for the latter? They are practically forgotten in the new budget presented this year. Young people are forgotten because family allowances are not increased; old people are forgotten, the unemployed and the farmers also. Who is remembered? That is where the highest increase is made, the interest on the public debt is taken care of. That is what the Minister of Finance keeps in mind.
In closing I will say that the Minister of Finance is doing his job well. He was chosen by Toronto's Bay street to help the financiers, and that is what he keeps on doing in his 1965 budget.

MR. NIELSEN-REQUEST FOR APPEARANCE BEFORE DORION COMMISSION-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
The question of privilege raised on Friday last by the hon. member for Yukon could perhaps be divided into three parts. The first one relates to the attendance of members in general. In this regard my attention was drawn to standing order 5, which reads as follows:
Every member is bound to attend the service of the house, unless leave of absence has been given him by the house.
In W. F. Dawson's volume entitled "Procedure in the Canadian House of Commons", at page 89 it will be seen that the above standing order has remained unchanged since confederation. For the first ten years of its life the House of Commons enforced this rule. A member who wished to leave Ottawa requested

leave through a colleague. Reasons for the absence were generally given, and examples may be found of the plea of "urgent private business", "family affliction", and "severe illness" to excuse a member from his duty. Although this rule still appears in our standing orders, it would seen that since 1877 the formal granting of leave of absence to a member of the house is a practice which has fallen into disuse.
Bourinot deals with the subject of attendance of members at page 153 of his fourth edition, in the following words:
Members of the Senate and House of Commons are expected to attend regularly in their places and perform their duties under the constitution In case of unavoidable absence it was formerly customary to have the reasons explained to the house, and leave given to the member to absent himself from his duties.
Then in the following paragraph he adds:
The practice in old Canada, as in England, was to have a call of the house and order all the members to attend on a particular day, but this practice has now become obsolete-no cases having occurred since 1867.
In the British house the formal granting of leave of absence to a member has also largely fallen into disuse, as will be seen by referring to page 369 of May's seventeenth edition. Very interesting historical notes as to the attendance in the house are to be found at pages 112, 113 and 114 of the second volume of "The Procedure of the House of Commons" by Redlich. This study is too long to be quoted here, although it confirms the view that the former practice has largely disappeared in the British house.
It might be well to underline here that with regard to standing order No. 5, as well as with regard to any other standing orders of the house, we must keep in mind paragraph 3 of citation 8 in Beauchesne's fourth edition, which reads as follows:
In the interpretation of the rules or standing orders the house is generally guided, not so much by the literal construction of the orders themselves as by the consideration of what has been the practice of the house with respect to them.
It is my view that I have today to interpret standing order 5 in the light of what has been the practice of the house with respect to it for so many decades, unless it would be the intention of the house to revive the old practice. Otherwise I would feel that I am deciding that many of us and of our predecessors since 1877 have, at one time or another, been guilty of contempt of parliament for having been in disobedience of an order of the house during that period.
Question of Privilege
The second point which the hon. member brought to my attention seems to relate to the attendance of members as witnesses outside parliament during a session, and he referred to May's fifteenth edition at page 121, where it is stated, in part, that "members of both houses are, by the law and custom of parliament, exempted from attendance as witnesses during the session of parliament".
May, in his seventeenth edition at page 76, deals with the privilege relating to members summoned as witnesses, in the following terms:
The service of a subpoena to attend as a witness has been treated as a breach of privilege by the house and the parties responsible for service have on occasions been committed to the Sergeant for contempt. It is doubtful, however, whether under present usage the actual service would as a general rule be regarded as a breach of privilege, unless effected within the precincts of the house, sedente domo, on the general principle of the service of civil process. But-
And I wish to stress this:
-the privilege of exemption of a member from attending as a witness has been asserted by the house upon the same principle as other personal privileges viz., the paramount right of parliament to the attendance and service of its members; and in certain cases on the matter being raised by the member concerned the Speaker has communicated with the court drawing attention to this privilege and asking that the member should be excused. On other occasions the Commons have granted leave to their members on the ground that their attendance as witnesses was required and have admitted the same excuse for defaulters at calls of the house-
Concerning the same matter, Campion in his third edition at page 64 makes the following statement, and once more I wish to stress the doctrine:
The doctrine that a member's attendance in the house takes precedence of all other obligations once enabled him to resist a subpoena to attend as a witness, but this privilege is now regularly waived.
In that regard, may I mention here that while the attendance of a member in the house is to be considered an obligation on the part of a member, the exemption from attending as a witness is to be considered as a privilege which attaches to members of parliament individually and which is derived from such obligation of attending the service of the house. It is my view that although the individual privilege of a member to be exempted from attending as a witness subsists, such a privilege, being based on the paramount right of parliament to the attendance and service of its members, an absence from the house for the purpose of attending as a witness should be dealt with in the same

Question of Privilege
manner as any other absences by members; and considering the practice followed in this house for many decades, I do not see that there is an urgent necessity for a member to obtain leave to attend as a witness unless it is intended to implement standing order 5 in all cases of absences of members.
The third part of this question of privilege, which seems to me entirely different from the two others, is to the effect that by the law of parliament no member is at liberty to give evidence elsewhere in relation to any debates or proceedings in parliament except by the leave of the house of which he is a member.
The hon. member has drawn my attention in particular to section 11 of the report of the select committee on the official secrets act in the British house during 1938-39, which appears at page 423 of Beauchesne's fourth edition.
May, at page 63 in his seventeenth edition, deals with evidence before the courts as to proceedings in parliament in the following terms:
The practice of the Commons regarding evidence sought for outside the walls of parliament touching proceedings which have occurred therein also conforms to article 9 of the bill of rights. This fact is well recognized by the courts, which have held that members cannot be compelled to give evidence regarding proceedings in the House of Commons without the permission of the house.
At page 62 of the same volume May gives the meaning of the term "proceedings in parliament", as follows:
The primary meaning, as a technical parliamentary term, of "proceedings" (which it had at least as early as the seventeenth century) is some formal action, usually a decision, taken by the house in its collective capacity. This is naturally extended to the forms of business in which the house takes action, and the whole process, the principal part of which is debate, by which it reaches a decision.
In reading in Hansard what was said last Friday, it would seem that the intention of the hon. member for Yukon would be to assist the commission in any way he can and that he would like to be at liberty, if necessary, to answer questions on matters which have, in one way or another, been before the house and not to be placed in a situation, should he be called up to do so, where he could not give evidence as to what has been said in the house.
Consideration has also been given by me to the fact that the matters dealt with by the Dorion commission have been many times referred to in this house, either in debate or otherwise; and I have borne in mind the

views expressed by the hon. member for Peace River, to the effect that there is an indication that it will be the intention of the commission counsel to examine the member for Yukon as to what he said in this house, and to that extent the Hansard record with respect to the statements he made might be the subject of considerable discussion and questioning when the commission resumes its proceedings.
In the light of those remarks, as well as in the light of the reference given by the hon. member for Yukon and the last quotation from May's seventeenth edition, I am of the opinion that the hon. member, in order to have complete freedom and also in order to avoid possible complaints of breach of privileges after he has given evidence, has grounds for requesting leave of the house to give evidence involving the proceedings in this house, and I would be inclined to consider the request for leave by the hon. member as arising out of a matter of privilege.
Therefore I would accept at this time a motion to the effect that the hon. member for Yukon be granted leave to give evidence before the Dorion commission in relation to debates and proceedings in parliament with regard to the things that may be dealt with in the inquiry.
On Friday last a motion was presented to the Chair by the hon. member for Greenwood. It would appear to me that the wording of that motion is hypothetical and irregular, since no members other than the member for Yukon have asked for leave to give evidence in relation to debates and proceedings of this house.
To summarize my view, I would say that in my opinion the matter which is to be considered as arising out of a matter of privilege is not, if we consider our practice, the member's request to obtain leave of absence from the house but rather the granting of leave for him to give evidence in relation to the debates and proceedings of this house.

Question of Privilege

MR. KNOWLES-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MR. KNOWLES-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of questions and answers in the House of Commons on Friday last, March 19. As reported at page 12574 of Hansard, I asked the Prime Minister certain questions regarding a report that Professor Mulford Q. Sibley was going to be denied entry into Canada for the purpose of delivering a lecture at a public meeting that was to be held in Winnipeg Friday evening. I asked my question just before the luncheon adjournment at one o'clock. The Prime Minister indicated that he would look into the matter during that adjournment. In fact he was very precise; he said he would look into it at five minutes past one.
When the house resumed at 2.30 I asked the Prime Minister, as recorded at page 12575 of Hansard, whether he had any further information regarding Professor Sibley. In his reply the Prime Minister indicated that he had made certain investigations during the luncheon recess and that those investigations were proceeding. He ended his statement with this sentence:
The man in question has not yet appeared at the border, and I hope that as a result of the investigation which has been made there will be no difficulty in this regard.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, it is generally known that even before the Prime Minister made that statement at half past two on Friday, Professor Sibley had already been questioned at Winnipeg and been given the option of either remaining in custody until a tribunal considered his case or returning to Minneapolis on the plane on which he had come.
Mr. Speaker, I am not alleging that the Prime Minister sought to mislead the house by the statement he made at half past two on Friday. In fact I must point out that I telephoned the Prime Minister's office about three o'clock Friday afternoon, and I was informed that the information he gave the house at half past two was the latest information he had received at that time from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, there is recorded in Hansard a statement which does not accord with the facts as they were at that time, and as a matter of privilege I feel that there should at least be a statement by the Prime Minister

Question of Privilege
reconciling what he said at 2.30 p.m. on Friday with the tact that Professor Sibley had already been sent back to the United States.
May I also point out that the Prime Minister on Friday said he hoped there would be no difficulty in this regard, namely in respect of the case of Professor Sibley, whereas press reports indicate that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration had given the order the day before that this professor was not to be allowed entry into Canada for the purpose of making the scheduled address. That is another point which it seems to me we should have reconciled.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, amongst others who had protested this action the governor of Minnesota, Karl Rolvaag, has issued a public protest declaring that what had happened was unbelievable. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that as a matter of privilege, when the governor of a state of another country complains about our denial of fundamental human freedom, we should have a statement about the matter from the Prime Minister.
If the Prime Minister responds to this question of privilege, as I hope he will, I hope he will also tell us whether the questioning of Professor Sibley and the refusal to allow him to come in was an isolated incident, or whether this is an established practice on the part of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Because I have raised this question as a matter of privilege, I have prepared an appropriate motion which would call for the matter to be referred to a committee for investigation and report, but I will refrain from putting that motion at this time. I will wait until Your Honour has heard other comments on the situation and has decided whether this is the kind of question of privilege which should be followed by a motion. In any case, in view of the various irreconcilable facts which I have recited, I hope the Prime Minister will attempt to reconcile them in order that the good name of Canada, as a place where we believe in freedom of speech, can be maintained.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: MR. KNOWLES-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to deal with the question of privilege, and that is all I have any right to deal with at this time.
I should like to say at the outset that I do not consider that a telegram of protest from the governor of a state in the United States necessarily means that there is a question of privilege before this House of Commons.

Some of the other observations made by the hon. gentleman I think are perfectly proper, but I am not sure they are proper in terms of the motion of privilege which the hon. gentleman is contemplating.
I am very glad indeed to deal with the matter he has raised because, as he pointed out, I did make the statement in the house on Friday that the man in question, Professor Sibley, had not yet appeared at the border. It is true that he had crossed the border at that time, but as my hon. friend has stated, he was not suggesting that I was deliberately misleading the house. If there had been a suggestion of that kind made I would be the first to move that this matter be referred to the committee on privileges and elections.
In order to clear away the difficulty to which he has made reference I should like to point out that after questions were interrupted on Friday by the luncheon recess, I returned to my office and asked for a full report in compliance with my undertaking. I did so immediately after one o'clock, and I received information from the department concerned through the head of the branch that Professor Sibley at that time had not reached Winnipeg, and that they did not know when he was coming to Winnipeg or, indeed, if he was coming.
That was all the information I had from 1.10 p.m. until 2.30 p.m., at which time I checked again before coming into the house. If the professor did not come to Winnipeg- and I was told by the department that there was not any information that he was in fact coming-then of course the difficulty would have been resolved. If he was coming later, which I thought was more likely, then I felt there would be time for me to look into the matter, examine the situation and perhaps resolve the difficulty in consultation with the minister.
When I returned to the house at 2.30 p.m., Mr. Speaker, that was the information I gave to my hon. friend who asked the question. That was exactly the information I had received from the department concerned. It is true that later-I think it was around three o'clock-I received information to the effect that Professor Sibley had indeed landed in Winnipeg, had been interviewed at the airport and given the alternative of appearing before a special committee of inquiry or returning at once to Minneapolis. He took the latter alternative and returned to Minneapolis. When I received that information the question

period had concluded in the House of Commons, so I conveyed it by telephone to my hon. friend.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, the minister had approved the order the day before that he be not admitted without a special examination or unless an organization made an application for his admission so the matter could be looked into at once. It is true that the minister made that decision on Thursday afternoon, or some time on Thursday.
So far as the times are concerned, I understand the aircraft reached Winnipeg airport at 1.20 p.m., eastern time, and that Professor Sibley was interviewed at once by the immigration official at the airport. I understand that interview continued until shortly after 2 p.m., at which time the professor boarded the same plane and returned to Minneapolis. I understand that the official of the department made a report to the department of immigration shortly after 2 p.m. He did so by first writing, no doubt for his own information, and then by telephoning the department. As soon as the department received that information they phoned my office and conveyed it to me, and as soon as I received it I conveyed the information to the hon. gentleman.

This house has a right to true and complete information. Let me point out the fact that the day before, on the Thursday, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration had apparently refused this man admission into Canada except if the person in question would qualify certain reservations. We have a right to know what those reservations were. What manner of man is this? What offence has he committed? What was the danger in allowing him to come into Canada?
Certainly the explanation by the Prime Minister adds a great deal more to the cloud of suspicion that Canadians as a whole feel regarding this incident. The house is entitled to a far better explanation than has been given up to the moment. I ask the Prime Minister to give it, rather than to be so supersensitive as to become annoyed immediately when there is any reference to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, which has certainly had a most unusually neglectful record in the last few months.
I ask the Prime Minister this. What offence had Sibley committed? What were his views that were going to be detrimental to the people of Canada? In what way would his presence here constitute a danger to the nation, for such must have been the fact? Whether or not you agree, certainly in the market place of ideas there is no reason, unless there are words of sedition or a record in that regard, to prevent a person from another country from coming into Canada and placing his views before a Canadian organization.

maintopic: MR. KNOWLES-DENIAL OF ENTRY TO U.S. PROFESSOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very carefully refrained from dealing with the question of substance because that was not the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The right hon. gentleman has, of course, gone beyond the question of privilege.

Question of Privilege
In regard to the question of substance I would say only this, and I have a right to say it because of what has been said. I have asked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to go to Winnipeg to investigate the circumstances surrounding this case and to return to Ottawa and report to me and also make a report to the House of Commons on the whole matter as soon as he gets back. He will be in Winnipeg looking into this matter later today.
With regard to one point raised by the right hon. gentleman on the question of privi-ledge, he twice made the allegation that the officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in Ottawa had held back the facts from me. That was the statement he made. In fairness to officials who cannot speak for themselves, and out of respect for the truth, Mr. Speaker, I say that statement is untrue. The officials of the immigration branch got the telephone call from the airport at Winnipeg after the plane had gone back. The official at Winnipeg had made his own notes and that telephone call was received in Ottawa at 2.45 p.m. So perhaps the right hon. gentleman will withdraw the allegation in fairness to the civil service.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Prime Minister owes the house a great deal more explanation than we have had so far. The Prime Minister has explained why he was not able to get the information at 2.30 on Friday that Professor Sibley had already been turned back at the border, and that he could not get that information from the civil service here in Ottawa. The fact is that the minister and presumably the department had already decided, the day before, that Professor Sibley was to be turned back at the border.
Does this mean that the minister and his senior officials had made this decision on Thursday, yet at 2.30 on Friday they did not know that this decision had been made and could not transmit it to the Prime Minister when he asked for this information? Either there is a complete breakdown of communication in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or there is a breakdown between the department and the Prime Minister's office. I say the Prime Minister owes the

house more explanation than to tell us that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will return to the house and give the house a full explanation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subtopic: INQUIRY INTO RELATIONSHIP OF PRICES, COSTS, ETC. TO ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recent increases in steel prices have raised the broader question of the relationship of prices, costs and incomes to sustained economic growth. The government's objective is to achieve high rates of such economic growth while maintaining a reasonable measure of price stability.
I believe that it would be useful to launch a broad examination into these matters. For that purpose we are fortunate in having in the economic council of Canada an agency which, by virtue of its terms of reference, its representation from all elements of the Canadian economy and its highly qualified staff, is suited for this kind of task.
The government is therefore requesting the economic council:
1.	To study factors affecting price determination and the interrelation between movements in prices and costs and levels of productivity and incomes.
2.	To report on their relationship to sustained economic growth and to the achievement of high levels of employment and trade and rising standards of living.
3.	To review the policies and experiences of other countries in this field and their relevance for Canada.
Canadian Economy

subtopic: INQUIRY INTO RELATIONSHIP OF PRICES, COSTS, ETC. TO ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext:
In connection with this announcement, I may say it was difficult to follow exactly what the government has decided because the statement was read rapidly by the Prime Minister. However, this looks to me like an endeavour on the part of the government to get rid of this whole question by simply a generalized placing before the economic council of the relationship of wages and prices and the contributing factors to increases in prices. This is a long way from what is needed today in connection with the situation relating to steel.
The increase in steel prices-I am not talking about its justification at the moment -can only lead to a widening and greater expansion of inflation. What the Prime Minister has done has been to brush it aside, as I see it, in a generalized form of presentation by asking the economic council to consider all phases of price relationship, rather than dealing with the question of steel which is a matter of first importance. I am sure the people as a whole will see that this is simply a means, a subterfuge if I may be allowed to use that expression, to get away from facing the situation regarding the increase in the price of steel.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subtopic: INQUIRY INTO RELATIONSHIP OF PRICES, COSTS, ETC. TO ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext:
I am glad the government is finally seized of the importance of the recent increase in the price of steel. I think it was about two weeks ago that I first raised this matter in the house. I contended then that the increase in price was both unwarranted and unjustified. Since that time there has been a steady stream of price increases by other steel companies which have followed the lead of the Steel Company of Canada. Undoubtedly this will have the effect of increasing the prices of commodities which have a steel content, particularly cars, appliances, building materials and so on.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when this matter was first raised the government took the position it was largely due to an increase in wages. I take it that position has been completely demolished, because since 1957 hourly earnings have increased by only about 26.5 per cent. This increase has not even kept pace with the increase in productivity, so that the labour cost of steel has declined by $5.36 per ton. Profits in the same period have been up 106 per cent for the Steel Company of Canada, which was the first company to increase the price.

Canadian Economy
The Prime Minister has taken the course of referring this matter to the economic council of Canada. One of the goals which the economic council set in their annual report was the stabilizing of prices over the period under consideration. Certainly if prices are going to remain reasonably stable-and the economic council set an annual increase in prices of 2 per cent-then this is a matter which must cause them a great deal of concern.
I have serious doubts, Mr. Speaker, as to whether the economic council of Canada is the body best equipped to make this kind of investigation. They are a body for collecting data and doing economic forecasting. This situation is going to require a very intense investigation, the calling of the steel company representatives and other persons who are interested, trade unions, the consumers of steel products, and investigations into the financial statements of the companies, labour costs and profits. I would have thought the government would have set up a royal commission to look into this matter.
I would have thought, too, the government would have asked the restrictive trade practices branch to see whether these increases which are being adopted by all the steel companies warranted some action under the restrictive trade practices legislation. There would seem, on the face of it, to be some indication of collusion and in price fixing.
It may be that an investigation by the economic council of Canada is better than nothing. However, I do not believe that this body is equipped to carry on this type of investigation or to make the kind of report which must be made speedily if any action is going to be taken. I point out that a report six months or eight months from now is worthless. This increase in the price of steel will have its economic repercussions over the entire economy.
The Financial Post recently published a long list of the various sectors of the economy that will be affected by this increase in the price of steel. A lengthy investigation by the economic council of Canada, along with all the other things it has to do, will not meet the situation which confronts the people of Canada. This requires a highly specialized and intensive study carried on immediately and recommending specific action by the government of Canada in order to prevent serious price increases right across the economy. I am of the opinion that the economic council of Canada is not likely to be able to make the kind of report

quickly enough and the kind of recommendations that will prevent this spiral of inflation which is undoubtedly going to follow the increases in the price of steel.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subtopic: INQUIRY INTO RELATIONSHIP OF PRICES, COSTS, ETC. TO ECONOMIC GROWTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a few words concerning the increase in the price of steel which the federal government is apparently going to accept and which, according to the previous speaker, would be due to the wage increase granted a few weeks ago.
Now, I agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) that wages alone cannot determine a price increase. Nevertheless, they are still partly responsible for the rise in the price of steel.
Increasing the company's profits requires or contributes to a general increase in the price of steel. Today the government is bringing forward a policy designed to have the Canadian people accept a general increase in the price of steel. But we have in Canada a body that can detect exactly where a trust exists.
I think that a combine exists in the steel production industry. The government should assume its responsibilities concerning this steel combine the purpose of which is to keep prices at a high level because, after all, this price increase will be paid by the Canadian consumers generally, even though the leader of the New Democratic party tells us that this increase is not solely due to wages. He nevertheless refers to the official paper of his party, the Financial Post, to point out that steel prices are set independently from wages paid.
But, in the final analysis, it is neither the government members nor the members of the opposition nor even the leader of the New Democratic party who will be paying the shot; it will be the Canadian consumer.
We say, Mr. Speaker, that this steel price increase, instead of being made in this way should be made by the government through the allowance of a compensated discount to steel producers so that consumers may pay less for needed facilities and products, such as automobiles, refrigerators, electrical appliances, in short, everything made of steel.
The government would then be discharging its duties better than it is doing now. Wages are included in prices, whether we want it or not; the pension benefits paid by industries are also included in prices. All plans, whatever they may be, are included in prices and, in the final analysis, it is the

consumers, the workers, the farmers and the people as a whole who are paying the administration or, if you wish, the distribution costs.
Our technique differs considerably from that of the government. It is up to the government to decide whether the increase in price granted to the steel industries will be more beneficial to the Canadian people than the compensated discount technique advocated by Social Credit for nearly 40 years.
I think the Prime Minister of Canada is indeed aware of the means we are suggesting. He knows very well that the means he is putting forward today to increase the steel prices will in no way solve the distribution problem in Canada. Let the right hon. Prime Minister and his cabinet work instead toward finding a better solution to the distribution of Canadian wealth for the people and among the people who are building Canada. Then, we shall give our unconditional support to the right hon. Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PENITENTIARY SENTENCE OF JOSEPH TREMBLAY, VANCOUVER
speechtext:
1. Robert Tremblay was sentenced to penitentiary on December 19, 1955 and on November 23, 1956.
2.	His trials took place in Vancouver and New Westminster, British Columbia.
3.	A first charge for attempted murder and a second charge for forcible seizure.
4.	He was sentenced to 20 years on the first charge and to 1 year consecutive on the second charge.
5.	6 and 7. Robert Tremblay was admitted to the British Columbia penitentiary on June 5, 1956. He was transferred to the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary on June 29, 1964 by authority of a removal warrant signed for the commissioner of penitentiaries by Mr. J. R. Stone, deputy commissioner of penitentiaries, on June 16, 1964.
This transfer was arranged in the following circumstances:
The deputy commissioner of penitentiaries was making a routine inspection of the institutions in British Columbia in February 1964. En route to the William Head institution, the warden of British Columbia penitentiary informed the deputy commissioner that Tremblay, after having been dissociated from the other inmates for over five years, had so changed his outlook that he was in the minimum security institution at William Head. However, he had requested to see the warden to ask for a transfer back to British Columbia penitentiary as he was unhappy in the open dormitory living at the William Head institution.

Questions
The deputy commissioner suggested to the warden that Tremblay should be staged through a medium security institution to prepare him for minimum security and, as there was no medium security prison in British Columbia, Tremblay, because he intended to live in Quebec after his release, should be transferred to St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary with the object of his eventual transfer to the Leclerc medium security institution. Tremblay requested a transfer to the Leclerc institution accordingly.
Making routine arrangements for the transfer and the fact that it would not be effected until an escort could be provided by officers from British Columbia coming east to attend staff college delayed the issue of the transfer authority until June 16, 1964.
This transfer was a routine one in the best interest of the inmate's rehabilitation and was effected without any outside pressure on the penitentiary authorities. No representations, either by letter or oral, were made to the Minister of Justice concerning it.

Mr. Speaker, I am informed by the Department of Trade and Commerce as follows:
The standards branch uses seals and stickers as evidence of inspection. Since these are used throughout Canada, it was felt desirable that where words appear on the seal or sticker these should be in both the English and French languages. The seal used for wax imprints under the Electricity Inspection Act and the Gas Inspection Act is relatively small so that, as a result of the incorporation of both languages, the crown design, if included, would have been rendered too small in size.
