speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the first things that comes to my mind with respect to Bill No. C-142 concerning the withdrawal from certain joint programs at the request of a province, is that the federal finance and national revenue departments will fortunately take less money from the pockets of Canadian taxpayers.
I am glad that the total budget of the Department of Finance will be reduced by that amount. And I am glad for this reason: the Department of Finance obviously does not know how to spend the money it collects from the Canadian taxpayers.
One of the remarks I made to myself when I examined the estimates tabled today is that it will cost $82,299,500 in salaries alone, or $82,300,000, to pay the income tax inspectors and officials, that is to say the employees who empty the citizens' pockets.
Therefore, I tell myself that if the federal government takes less, the Department of National Revenue will need fewer employees and on this item of $82,300,000 alone the Minister of Finance will realize quite a sav-

ing. Let us hope that by reducing the staff of the income tax office, since the federal government will collect less money, the Minister of Finance will make a saving there.
When I examine the estimates which were tabled today and compare them with the various joint programs-those that Quebec at least will opt out of-I can only conclude that it will be a good thing for Quebec because the federal government never learned or at least never had enough imagination to learn how to spend the taxpayers' money.
For instance, for the class which is, at this time, the most handicapped, the most depressed, the most mistreated by our governments, that is the agricultural class, I find that the total expenditures of the federal government during the year will amount to $121 million, while the budget of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reaches the record figure of $99,444,000, a difference of only $20 million; $121 million for agriculture and $100 million for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is therefore easy to conclude that the Department of Finance does not take priorities into account. That is why I am happy to see that more money will be taken from the federal Department of Finance, because it does not know how to manage the taxpayers' money.
When you read, for instance, that the Department of External Affairs will be spending the sum of $133 million during the year, that is $12 million more than for agriculture, it is easy to see that the Department of Finance does not know how to allocate proper amounts to the various departments.
In the field of labour, for example, where last year you had a sum of $186 million, we find that this year only $150 million is to be spent. If there is an important department, it is the Department of Labour. When you look at the unemployment situation and the number of jobless people, you know how important the Department of Labour is if we want to try and find work for our Canadian citizens. But no, its estimates are being cut.
So, what does my heart the most good is to realize that the Minister of Finance, who does not know how to spend the taxpayers' money, will have less to look after, so that the evil will be less great. I am not saying it will disappear, but it will be smaller.
Mr. Speaker, another reason why I support the opting out formula under which a province may withdraw from joint programs- and it is said that many provinces wish to so withdraw-is that all those shared pro-20220-801
Dominion-Provincial Relations grams are administered by both the federal and provincial governments and, consequently, for the whole of Canada, there is a duplication of administrative services and you have two systems and twice as many employees, some in Ottawa and others in the provincial governments, in the fields of administration, accountancy, audit and inspection.
Therefore, it costs twice as much as if the administration and operation of the joint programs came under a single administration. Furthermore, because of this dual administration, decisions concerning joint programs will be delayed considerably; for instance, should a municipality decide to undertake winter works programs, it will have to apply to the provincial government, then after the provincial government makes some inspections and inquiries, etc., and approves the programs, the whole matter is referred to the federal government which makes its own inspections and inquiries and this takes twice as much time.
It takes twice the amount of time required to reach a decision when you have two administrations, one provincial and the other federal, while the provincial administration would be able to make its own decisions.
This, therefore, slows down the grants for winter works to the municipalities and it costs twice as much as a result of an overlapping system of bureaucracy. In addition to delaying the decisions, we realize that often there is disagreement between the decisions of the federal and provincial authorities.
I have seen, in my riding of Lapointe, the federal government decide in favour of a municipality with regard to winter works; later on, the provincial authorities would decide otherwise so that the municipality had to wait for two or two and a half years before getting its grant. On other occasions, the federal authorities refuse to make a decision so that the municipalities do not know where they stand, they are always on a tight rope. This situation works hardship on the municipalities, because some decisions are delayed and here again the municipalities, the workers and the unemployed are the first to suffer therefrom.
That is why I say that those joint programs with their dual authority, a dual bureaucratic system of auditing and inspection, double expenditures, a double system of management, are a disastrous invention for the administration and the taxpayers. It cost them money and resulted in the provinces being deprived of a great part of their auton-

Dominion-Provincial Relations omy. This system has given no positive results, except delayed decisions where the two authorities concerned are often at cross purpose.
Mr. Speaker, the best thing the federal government could do with regard to opting out arrangements would be to hand back to the provinces, in no uncertain way, and undoubtedly to the province of Quebec, sources of revenue equal to the amounts spent in the various joint programs, so the provinces themselves may collect the revenues and taxes and administer what were formerly joint plans.
However, if we admit this principle, there are in Bill C-142 certain provisions which could be improved. Quite often it is the role of the opposition to make suggestions so as to improve a bill of this nature. In my opinion, here is the most important improvement which should be brought to Bill C-142: Under its provisions, the federal government retains the right to audit and inspect the records of the provinces which will administer those programs themselves. The federal government is giving something away, but it retains a measure of control in order to inspect and check those joint programs.
Mr. Speaker, that is not acceptable because the provinces are now clearly capable of administering themselves. All the more so since those fields belong to provincial jurisdictions under the British North America Act.
The provinces will have sufficient income to carry on the implementation of those projects. Then, why should the federal government, which will no longer collect the taxes, which will no longer be there to pass and administer regulations, continue to interfere in provincial matters through inspection, auditing and control when the provinces no longer need the federal government?
Let the federal government start by auditing itself, inspecting itself, before auditing and inspecting what concerns other governments that have no need for such interference by the federal authority in provincial matters.
There is for instance the hospital insurance plan. The provinces must be in a position- and they are capable of doing so-to administer their own plans, to select their projects, to provide the services that they wish, without having to answer to federal authorities. What the Minister of Finance is now doing is to give and hold back at the same time, since he keeps a right of control, of auditing, of inspection of those plans.

Why always try to hold at the end of a string or a chain the provincial authorities which are clearly capable of administering in their own areas?
Mr. Speaker, this makes it all the more necessary to give back to the provinces, without conditions or restrictions, the sources of income they need to be in a position to decide for themselves which plans they want to introduce according to various regions, and we know that regions differ greatly in Canada, that all regions do not have the same problems. Then why not give back to the provinces the sources of income they need? Why not leave it up to the provinces, giving them the necessary authority, to decide what plans they will implement in their territory, what plans they will put the emphasis on, what plans they need more than others.
Let the provinces take such decisions and give them back the sources of income they are entitled to under the Canadian constitution. Let the provinces select themselves their plans and priorities as they wish.
Of course, in certain areas, there will be provinces that are behind, and in other areas, the same provinces will be ahead. Then, in the areas where the province lags behind, greater sums of money will be provided at its discretion because, after all, the elected representatives of the people are the ones to decide about it.
I notice, for instance, that the federal government clearly interferes in the field of education. It has even given instructions. Here is what one can read in this bill:
(a)	vocational high school training;
(b)	technical training;
(c)	training of the disabled;
(d)	training of technical and vocational teachers;
(e)	student aid;
(f)	technical and vocational correspondence courses;
(g)	that part of the trade and occupational training program that does not relate to the training of persons who are already members of the labour force.
Those are all points on which the federal government has infringed upon the field of education in the past few years.
If Quebec wishes to appropriate more funds to other programs, if it feels that a priority need is involved, it should be free to make a choice all by itself.
In that way the provinces will be getting back a fair percentage of the income tax equivalent to joint programs, for the needs of the provinces are greater than those of the federal government at present.

When I look at the expenditures of the federal government, I feel it is scandalous for Ottav/a to take such a large share of our tax dollar when it does little with it for the Canadian people. For the Department of Finance alone an enormous amount, $1,712 million, is spent. The Canadian people get absolutely nothing out of that.
I see, for instance, that debt charges amount to $1,101 million. That does not give the Canadian people anything either.
I notice that the R.C.M.P. costs us $75,927,000 even though our needs are much greater in other fields, for instance in agriculture. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration costs $92,279,000 a year whereas nothing is done to help farmers get out of the slump in which they are right now. Such expenditures for federal departments are a scandal. In fact, it goes beyond any understanding that an agency like the economic council of Canada should get only $990,000, not even a million, when it has to encourage the establishment of new industries and promote economic development in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we note, for instance, that the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, one of the most important departments, have been reduced by $19 million, and in order to increase what? The public debt charges. The same is true of the C.B.C., the R.C.M.P. and the taxation division estimates.
That is how the Minister of Finance is spending our money, when the provinces have ever increasing needs directly affecting the Canadian people, even every individual. That is why we want the federal government to withdraw increasingly from taxation fields, so as to leave them to the provincial governments.
This afternoon I heard the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton)-that tickled me somewhat-ask how Quebec would be able to solve and finance by itself its educational problem. My answer to that is this. Do not worry, the province of Quebec is as able as any other Canadian province to solve its educational problem and to set up an educational system which will compare favourably with any other in the world. The province of Quebec is able to do that.
Now, it is asked also: How would the province of Quebec be able to finance such a system by itself? It could probably not do so in the past, because Ottawa used to come and take all the money. Then, there was nothing left for Quebec. But when the sources of revenue from personal and corporate in-20220-801J
Dominion-Provincial Relations come taxes are given back to Quebec, then there will be no reason to worry.
It is obvious that as long as Ottawa holds the purse strings, with Quebec having practically nothing, it will not be able to finance its educational system. But if they let Quebec collect its own taxes, then nobody in this house will wonder how Quebec will be able to solve and finance its educational problem.
Mr. Speaker, I have enough confidence in our university teachers, our educators in the province of Quebec, in short in the educational system which is being set up, to know that Quebec is able to set up an educational system which will be as good as that of any other country in the world. In fact, I am surprised by the fact that people always ask why Quebec would not be able to create an adequate system of education. I am of the opinion that there are in Quebec people able to set up a system which will be the pride of all Canada and all Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of the debate on the bill concerning the withdrawal of the federal government from certain joint programs, it has been asked whether such a withdrawal would affect Canadian unity. It has been asked how this unity will be preserved if the provinces opt out from these shared programs.
Mr. Speaker, I have always said and I still maintain that the only way to restore, not unity because that would be a chimerical dream, but goodwill in Canada, is that everyone should mind his own business.
Quebec's business is education, highways, health, natural resources and other fields granted to the provinces under the British North America Act. The federal government should stop minding Quebec's business; Quebec should be free to look after its own business and should get back the sources of income to which it is entitled.
When Ottawa starts minding its own business and stops encroaching continually on fields of provincial jurisdiction, then goodwill will be possible in Canada, but not otherwise. In fact, as long as the federal government keeps on guiding and directing Quebec as if it were a child, goodwill will not be possible, because we will never again accept the tutelage of a central government in fields coming under the exclusive jurisdiction of the province of Quebec, according to the British North America Act.
All the problems facing us today arise from the fact that all levels of government are trying to find sources of income. Municipali-

Dominion-Provincial Relations ties, school boards, provincial governments, the federal government, all are looking for sources of income and all of them have decided to take it from the only possible place, that is the taxpayers' pockets.
All governments lack imagination when it comes to trying to find some other source of revenue or another place where to seek the necessary funds to finance shared programs and especially hospital insurance, education and even public works. All lack imagination when it comes to finding sources of revenue elsewhere than in the pockets of the Canadian citizens. We can see the governments, at all levels, trying to outdo one another in drawing money from the taxpayer and the taxpayer is always the one who has to pay the shot.
How many new taxes were imposed or how many times were the taxes increased since this government came into power? In the field of building materials, for instance, the increase went as far as 11 per cent and never, except once, was the Minister of Finance able to find sources of revenue elsewhere than in the pockets of the taxpayer.
Once, he thought it advisable to use the Bank of Canada to help England. But for Canadians, no. He made a direct loan to England through the Bank of Canada. Why does not the Minister of Finance allow provincial governments to borrow directly from the Bank of Canada, with charges limited to management cost, the amounts needed for the development of the Canadian economy?
The minister has allowed the Bank of Canada to lend money to England to save the pound sterling. Would it not be more important to save the Canadian farmer who is suffering dire hardship? Would it not be also more important to save the Canadian unemployed who become every day more discouraged and more distressed in their own country? But the Minister of Finance does not think of that. To save England or the pound sterling, yes. But for the Canadian citizens, never.
Social credit for Britain, that is fine. But Canadians have to be satisfied with bank credit, the credit provided by big capitalists and that you borrow at high interest rates. And what does the Minister, of Finance do each year? He skips over that. He merely refers to it in passing, a matter of 20 seconds perhaps. I am even wondering if he did mention, seeing how unimportant it is to him, that the government would pay the fantastic sum of $1,100 million in debt interest charges alone. And we accept that. The Minister of Finance does not spend much

time on that. He goes over that very quickly.
Mr. Speaker, as long as we have a government that only thinks in terms of big capitalists, the Canadian people will react as they do today and demand some changes.
We shall accept, in principle, the opting out policy for shared cost programs, while being opposed to all those ropes with which the federal government wants to tie up the administration of those programs, one of which consists in checking the books as far as the implementation of such programs is concerned.
We say to the government that by attempting to solve problems of a public nature by way of taxes, it will make the people poorer. We suggest instead the use of the Bank of Canada to lend money to every public organization in need of capital to set those programs which were joint programs in the past.
As health insurance is on its way in, why not use the Bank of Canada to finance the plan under which every Canadian citizen could go to the doctor, the surgeon or the druggist without running into debt as he does today?
We are suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government and the finance department withdraw as quickly as possible from those taxation fields. They should stop impoverishing the people. They should rather utilize a means at their disposal, that is the Bank of Canada, to finance education, health insurance, hospital insurance, pension plans, unemployment assistance, public works. Canada would be far better off and there would be expansion of the economy instead of the government and the people steadily going into debt, and taxes would not increase constantly. The Canadian people are not getting any richer this way; they are getting poorer.
I think the government is not discharging its responsibilities as long as it is not creating the necessary credit to foster a greater economic growth and a greater development of our natural resources.
We accept this in principle, but we find, once again, that the government is not assuming its responsibilities in controlling finance in order to permit the Canadian people to benefit from the country's natural resources.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
subsubtopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) spoke this afternoon he mentioned the uneasy feeling which exists in the country over federal-provincial relations. This is understandable

because it is a very complex matter. It is understandable also because various people, including the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) have been stressing some of the problems of this relationship, particularly that of Quebec within confederation. Some segments of the press have also been playing with opting out, interpreting that phrase in a rather unfortunate way. It is therefore my purpose this evening to go briefly over the subject and try to put it in a better perspective, certainly a more positive perspective.
First, there is the general concept of conditional grants, and I want to define in a very loose but I think useful way what conditional grants are. They are grants from the federal treasury to the provinces, with some strings attached. They differ therefore in an important way from unconditional grants, which are grants from the federal treasury to the provinces with no strings attached. The provinces can choose their own priorities.
I believe we must continue to have conditional grants in this country-unconditional grants to help equalize opportunities for Canadians across the country-but conditional grants from Ottawa, with strings attached, in order to set certain national standards and make this a more viable country.
In economic terms there are at least three prerequisites to a nation. One is the free movement of goods and services throughout the country. In other words we must have in this half continent a common market, with free trade between the provinces. We also must have the free movement of money, or capital, and in order to ensure that we continue to have this we must have only one set of banking institutions. Canada, the nation, must insist on retaining federal control, national control, the control it has under the British North America Act, over money and banking.
Number three is that we must have certain standards, minimum standards across the country which will enable people to move more freely throughout Canada from job to job, to have greater opportunities and more even opportunities from province to province.
These are the three basic economic criteria-free movement of goods, free movement of money, and free movement of people, or greater mobility. In order to have this greater mobility we move essentially into areas of federal-provincial, and indeed provincial jurisdiction, into areas of highways, health, employment, or measures to promote more employment, and certain municipal services. Mobility in this sense is immensely im-
Dominion-Provincial Relations portant and there must be co-operation between the provinces and the nation.
As I have said before, this is a complex problem. Many countries, notably the United Kingdom, basically have only two levels of government, national and municipal. In this country to look after our varied and extensive territories and our regional differences we have provincial governments as well. We have three levels of government, and it is important that the powers of the provinces and the powers of the nation be properly defined. Conditional grants meanwhile have helped to make our constitution a more flexible one. In legal terms at least our constitution has not been modified greatly in the last 97 years. I hope that with the repatriation of the constitution it will be easier to do this in the future, but in the meantime the real effect of the division of powers in Canada has been bent and moulded to a considerable extent through the use of conditional grants.
Historically there are two basic approaches, widely different approaches, to conditional grants. One was the approach taken after the very exhaustive surveys of the Rowell-Sirois commission in the late thirties; the commission which was established as the result of the great depression and the concern about the inability of many provinces to finance the responsibilities which fall to them under the B.N.A. Act.
As I recall it, the Rowell-Sirois commission was not enamoured of conditional grants. It believed quite strongly in unconditional grants. It believed that the taxing powers in the main should be transferred to the federal government, that an equalization grant be given to each province, and that these grants be sufficient, so that the provinces in a relatively uniform manner could carry out all those responsibilities which fall to them under the B.N.A. Act.
The federal-provincial conference of 1942 discussed the Rowell-Sirois commission recommendations. The premiers of the provinces were not very enthusiastic, and the government of the day subsequently took a different tack in the so-called green book proposals of 1945. These consisted of a series of conditional grants pertaining to a very wide range of subjects falling within areas of provincial jurisdiction as outlined in the B.N.A. Act. Again that federal-provincial conference did not get very far.
A swing therefore took place from the Rowell-Sirois commission emphasis on unconditional grants to the green book pro-

Dominion-Provincial Relations posals, emphasizing conditional grants in the post-war reconstruction period. Each could have resulted in wide ranging agreements between the nation and the provinces.
In the years between 1946 and 1960 in an ad hoc, piecemeal way a large number of conditional grants were in fact set up. In other words, a good many of the green book proposals in the reconstruction era at the end of the war were in fact put into effect.
These proposals, mainly brought in by the King and St. Laurent governments, but added to by the Diefenbaker administration, helped to cement federal-provincial relations by resorting to conditional grants in a big way. Indeed it was not until the federal-provincial conference of 1960 that the provinces began to exhibit some real misgivings as to the nature and extent, particularly the extent, of conditional grants.
I understand that in 1957 the conditional grants amounted in total only to about $111 million. I say only, because by 1960-61 they were up to some $390 million, and since they have gone up and up and are now approaching the level of $1 billion. Obviously conditional grants have become very important in the post-war era. They have become in some respects onerous to the provinces, particularly with respect to the way in which the federal government requires the provinces to live up to certain standards.
I wish to refer briefly to the attitudes of the premiers of the provinces during the 1960 federal-provincial conference. I quote Premier Roblin of Manitoba from a booklet which I recommend to all hon. members, "Conditional Grants and Canadian Federalism," written by Donald V. Smiley of the University of British Columbia and published by the Canadian tax foundation in 1963. Premier Roblin is quoted on page 13 of this booklet as follows:
"We remain convinced.. .that some of the programs at least, initiated as they often are from the centre, place a sometimes onerous burden upon provincial and local finances at times when these local resources are least able to bear even the share of the total program costs left to them..."
Two of the premiers pointed out the administrative rigidities inherent in the existing grant arrangements. Premier Shaw commented that grants imparted "a degree of rigidity in the direction of provincial expenditures and reduce budgetary flexibility" as well as acting as a deterrent to long term budgetary planning by introducing uncertainties attendant upon future federal action in embarking on new programs or expanding existing ones.
Premier Douglas of Saskatchewan also spoke of the "rigidities" in the narrow definitions of aided activities. Both premiers suggested the possible

replacement of the present arrangements by "block" grants for broad areas of provincial activity.
I want to refer briefly to statements by two other premiers, Premier Manning of Alberta and Premier Lesage of Quebec. They attacked conditional grants on more clearly ideological grounds. Premier Manning, for example asserted.
These shared cost programs, particularly in the field of social services, of necessity transfer policy decisions from the legislatures of the respective provinces to the parliament and government of Canada. If the government of Canada decides that a certain form of health program or medical program... is desirable and is the type of program to which they are prepared to contribute, the provinces are then put in a position where no longer as legislators they decide as a matter of provincial policy that this is the type of social service their people require or desire, but rather their status is reduced to the mere right to decide whether or not they will participate in a program that already has been decided at the federal level.
I am looking for some notes here, Mr. Speaker, to which I wanted to refer, but perhaps I had better go on without reading. I wanted to refer to the position taken, first by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in a speech which he gave in Quebec city late in the fall of 1961. He outlined substantially the approach that is being taken in the present legislation. He, in effect, said that provinces should be permitted to contract out of programs which were well established and continuing in nature. He also went on to say that new initiatives would be taken and should be taken along the line of conditional grants and that these new programs should, in the main, have a limited duration; they should be introduced but for a specific period of time. In connection with those provinces which for various reasons, and particularly in the area of cultural activities, decided not to participate, they would not suffer any financial disability as a result of these arrangements. This, I believe, was the intent of the statement and this has substantially been followed in the current legislation.
I find also that in that year the New Democratic party, at its founding convention, paid a good deal of attention to federal-provincial relations. It came out in favour of dropping certain continuing programs, that is it provided for opting out. It also recommended the establishment of new programs, as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) has emphasized today. So I do not see that the New Democratic party, at least in its platform as adopted and enunciated in 1961, can argue very vociferously against the provisions of the current bill.

The present legislation is limited. It is limited in time to the period through to 1967-70. It deals only with established conditional grant programs. These established programs are ones which have been in existence for a considerable period of years, and they are ones which have become effectively imbedded in the fabric of our provincial administration in this country. A province which chooses to contract out of these programs, to in effect raise its own taxes to pay for them, will in the very nature of things be carrying on that program under its own auspices. In my view nothing is lost. Perhaps something is gained. The province in question will at least be taking on the responsibility of raising the taxes, raising the revenue, which it is spending in order to carry out these continuing programs.
The legislation as embraced in Bill No. C-142 also requires the provinces, under clause 3(2), to provide Ottawa with an accounting of the expenditures, so that during this interim period there is at least a measure of federal control. There is some measure of consolidation of the programs, but basically these programs continue on as they would have done, without change.
There are variable items in these financial arrangements. The ones which can be changed from time to time, such as capital investment, new construction and research have been retained by the federal government. In other words, the more variable elements, the more variable budgetary items have been retained by Ottawa. It is only the continuing programs, the ones in which there is a continuing, steady, consistent financial outlay which are available to the provinces which opt out, or contract out of these particular plans.
I think it is important to stress that nowhere has Ottawa given up its initiative in respect of these programs, programs which in the main are in the provincial area of responsibility. Ottawa, in my view, is not restricted in any way from embarking upon a national health program, programs for additional research assistance for the universities, on a second trans-Canada highway, and so on. These are not inhibited in any way by the current legislation. So those who would have Ottawa take the initiative in these important fields do not have to worry.
For those who think in terms of influencing the business cycle, or fiscal control, it is important to keep the total dollar values in some perspective. The federal budget is currently approaching $8 billion. During the last
Dominion-Provincial Relations year or so the provinces, in total, have had budgets passing that amount. In other words, the provinces collectively are financially now more important than Ottawa. Our continuing conditional grant arrangements meanwhile are now of the order of $1 billion. This is the amount of money, the degree of financial responsibility which is available to the province or provinces which collectively decide to take up this option and run these programs on their own. In other words, Ottawa is not giving up all its obligations. It is offering to give up a maximum of one eighth. And it is giving up the continuing elements, the consistent, stable elements; not the highly variable ones. So Ottawa is clearly maintaining the measure of control which is vital in respect of fiscal matters and monetary affairs.
There is another aspect to which I should like to refer briefly. These continuing programs, these conditional grants programs, which have become well established in the provinces which have come up to the specifications set by Ottawa, will over the years constitute a declining percentage of the total outlays of government. To the extent that they constitute a declining percentage of the total outlays of government they will call for a declining number of points in the personal income tax scale. In other words, where Ottawa has to move over by a given number of points today in order to turn over not only the responsibility but the resources necessary to finance these programs in the provinces, a lesser number of percentage points in the income tax scale will be required in ten years time, a still lesser number of percentage points in 20 years time, and so on. These continuing programs will become relatively less important with the passage of time. Hence Ottawa is not only turning over a fixed financial responsibility but is turning over programs which will diminish in the total picture and become less important in the over-all scheme of things.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has introduced an amendment. In effect, this amendment would refer the matters discussed in Bill No. C-142 back to yet another federal-provincial conference. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) says, there has already been 25 such conferences large and small over the last two years. We have had a lot of them. The hon. member for Edmonton West was most sarcastic a few months ago, I remember, claiming that we had a fourth level of govern-

Dominion-Provincial Relations ment in this country, a level of government which consisted of federal-provincial conferences. He thought this was a bad thing. But he is obviously falling into his own trap by advocating that we have yet another federal-provincial conference to resolve a matter which has been discussed and resolved between the federal authority and the provinces in recent months.
I think we must all be concerned about priorities, and the word "priorities" is mentioned in the amendment. The priorities today are shifting toward education, employment, health and municipal services. These in the main are responsibilities which under the B.N.A. Act belong to the provinces. In other words, priorities in expenditure are shifting toward the provinces. This is one of the reasons that a federal-provincial tax structure committee has been set up. It was set up last fall. It will be making interim reports, one this summer, and a final report, I understand, late in 1966. It will be exploring needs, establishing priorities, priorities not just purely provincial or purely federal, but covering the entire spectrum of federal-provincial affairs. It will be looking for tax sources and at methods of taxation. In other words, it will look at the obligations, the global picture of obligations, on the one hand, and at the sum total of tax resources on the other.
This tax structure committee will, I trust, come up with some of the answers. I trust that by 1967, as a result of this federal-provincial committee's work, we will have something akin to the Rowell-Sirois report of 1940 or the green book proposals of 1945. At least the approach will be comprehensive and there will be a meaningful analysis of the problems, a pattern toward which future legislation can be directed, which will sort out some of the uncertainties and a great many of the complexities which exist in federal-provincial financial and other arrangements.
I believe that in order for a democracy to work effectively, government has to be understandable. This is difficult in a federal system because of the several levels of government. I believe government must also be predictable. It must not only know where it is going, but it must indicate to everyone, private, public and departmental, where it is going. I think that as a result of this federal-provincial tax conference, we will get some of the guidelines prepared for us, and I trust it will be possible to follow these toward goals which many of us agree are desirable.


I trust too that there will be a reasonably clear division of responsibilities between the provinces on the one hand, the federal government on the other. As a result of constitutional changes we will, in a formal way, reallocate some of these responsibilities. But I am certain that conditional grants, new ones presumably, will also be needed in order to help carry out this process and help to distribute the wealth from the richer provinces in some measure to the less fortunate areas of the country. As for new initiatives, I trust future federal governments will be discussing them carefully and conclusively with the provinces before they are finalized and brought in as legislation.
I trust that the provinces will have an opportunity not to contract out-and I think the term is unfortunate-but to contract into these conditional grant programs across the country. Then it will be obvious to all that this is a nation building process. This is a process of setting up minimum standards of education and maximizing the opportunities for the youth of the country, providing pension and health benefits which enable people to move more freely around the country-in effect to give greater opportunities to all Canadians to really be Canadian in a united country.
Personally-and I am speaking personally throughout most of these remarks-I believe in a strong united Canada and in a Canada in which the national government takes on the task of giving strong and resolute leadership. In this dynamic federalism the national government may be creating new conditional grants programs from time to time. I trust also that it will be getting out of others. In effect, it will be possible for provinces to contract out of some and into other programs. I trust that all of them will contract in to all of the new programs, that is with rare exceptions. Also, as these programs age, and as they become established and part of the financial and social fabric of the country, I hope it will be possible for the federal government to give up its responsibility for policing these programs. The provinces will take them on on their own initiative, and they will become part and parcel of the provincial responsibilities both in respect to spending the money and raising it.
This is what Bill No. C-142 gives us a glimpse of. It does not set up an over-all pattern, but it certainly give us a glimpse of the possibility of a flexible arrangement whereby we can initiate new programs and eventually

let them rest at the proper level of governmental responsibility in this country.
That, then, is my main message. I think we can have a united Canada, a more flexible country, a country which is substantially a common market for goods and services and for money. I think we will see people becoming increasingly mobile throughout the length and breadth of Canada. I trust that the responsibilities of the provinces will be increasingly assumed by the provinces. But in the process the federal government will be showing many of the initiatives, initiatives which are nation-wide in scope and which make the country more of a unit, more of an entity and more of a nation as time goes by.

speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, most of these programs, and as I understand it virtually all of them, fall within provincial jurisdiction. This will make it possible for the provinces to properly assume their responsibilities. The federal government has made it possible to finance a program earlier in most cases than would otherwise have been the case. One reason a province may wish to do this is to publicly exert its rights under the British North America Act. In other cases it is administratively easier to do it this way. I have heard it said in some quarters that it would be preferable to administer these programs entirely within a province. There may be other reasons involved, but those are the two I can think of offhand.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the terminology is poor, because Canadians should think more in terms of positive measures. The term "contracting out" is one which has been used widely across the country. The term "contracting in", in respect of the future, pre-supposes that the federal government will negotiate and define future conditional grant programs, and then ask the provinces whether they wish to contract into them or not. If they follow the form of existing programs which deal with matters largely in the area of provincial responsibility, but into which the federal government has moved, I suggest that it should tread lightly, because the provinces have the right to stay in or stay out. Under those circumstances I suggest the provinces will in effect contract in.

speechtext: I do not agree with that statement. Let me state that I should like to see our constitution evolve. I should like to see the appropriate levels of government taking the responsibility for raising the money and spending it. Surely that is the only meaningful system that we can have; and in this regard I believe our constitution must evolve, in which case some of the responsibility should shift to the federal government. At the present time we have no flexibility whatever in the constitution, and conditional grants have afforded a means by which we have been able partially to get around the problem. I think in future, through a change in responsibility, there will be a shifting from one level of government to another, enabling everyone to deal more appropriately with these problems.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in winding up his remarks, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) said that his colleagues were in favour of a united Canada with a strong central government. I should like to associate myself most emphatically with that sentiment. A united Canada is what we need, and I am sure what every member of this chamber is working toward. There may be honest differences of opinion as to how we can best promote unity in this country, but in a discussion of the amendment to Bill C-142 we should have a right and a duty to express ourselves frankly and honestly to the end that we may promote that national unity in this country which we all want.
Bill C-142 is of great importance. It marks a fundamental change in the attitude of the provinces toward a strong central government, and for that reason we should be very careful in processing this legislation. I am wholeheartedly in support of the amendment which has been moved to the effect that this legislation should not be proceeded with further at this time until there has been an opportunity for a full review by a competent authority of the whole field of federal-provincial relationships.
We might refresh our minds by reading the amendment:
That Bill C-142 be not read a second time until further consideration has been given to the priorities of their requirements desired by the provinces of Canada and its territories in those fields of jurisdiction indicated in the schedules of the said bill, such priorities to be established at a federal-provincial conference convened for the said purpose.
In order to understand the amendment it might be wise to take a look at the thinking and reasoning behind the bill. To do this we can go back for a number of years in our history to about the time of world war II when these shared programs began. In introducing the legislation the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) pointed out quite well the reasons for these shared programs and said on March 17 last, as found on page 12482 of Hansard:
Shared cost programs have been evolved over the years to meet a variety of specific needs such as the provision of basic welfare services, basic health services, requirements for economic development and, in some cases, problems which, although temporary or local, were beyond the capacity of local resources.
He went on to point out that these needs have been met over the years. He said:
The provinces obtained the financial assistance that was necessary to enable them to provide

such services and at the same time it ensured a basic standard of services across Canada. The value of this approach in meeting these needs is evidenced by the number, scope and size of the current programs. In the current year such programs are expected to involve federal transfers to the provinces of more than $900 million, a substantial measure of assistance to governments whose level of expenditures has been rising rapidly in recent years.
Then he went on to point out why he thinks the reasons for these shared cost programs no longer exist and said that possibly we should now cancel them. He pointed out that these programs fall for the most part, or altogether, under provincial jurisdiction. With that I think everyone is prepared to agree. Then he went on to say:
Second, one of the fundamental problems which gave rise to these programs-that of unequal fiscal capacity among the various provinces -has been overcome to a considerable extent by the present system of equalization payments. Third, certain programs, such as hospital insurance, blind persons and disabled persons allowances, are mature and well established, and it is inconceivable that they would be discontinued by any government. Finally, conditional fiscal transfers have reached such a magnitude that one must consider the wisdom of continuing to separate responsibility for administering and spending large sums of money from the responsibility of raising the revenues. In the light of these and other developments which I enumerated in my speech on the resolution the case for continued federal participation in established joint programs is not as strong as it used to be.
He points out that these shared cost programs were entered into as a means of spreading the benefits of our national production in a better way, and I would liken them to the grants which are paid by provinces to municipalities. Through government grants the weaker municipalities are aided by the stronger municipalities and through these cost sharing programs the weaker economic areas of Canada have been assisted and helped by the stronger economic areas of Canada.
Take provinces like Ontario and Quebec in which are located many of the head offices of companies which draw revenue from all across the country. It would be unfair if provinces far distant from Toronto, for instance, which send large sums of money to the city of Toronto, had to finance their own services while the city of Toronto, drawing revenue from all across the country, was permitted to tax the head offices of these companies and thereby gain great revenue. If all that revenue were'left with that city to spend on its own services it would be grossly unfair. Therefore through the federal system of paying grants to provinces and through these shared cost programs, which have the same effect in our 20220-802J
Dominion-Provincial Relations national economy, the weaker areas of Canada have been helped by the stronger areas.
I contend that this need is just as great today as it was when these shared cost programs were begun. Considerable credit is due the former Conservative government because they greatly increased federal grants to provinces and to the less favoured areas of the country. The increased grants together with the shared cost programs have had the effect of standardizing services all across the country.
For 98 years this country has been able to get along very well under the British North America Act, which gave certain responsibilities to the provinces and certain responsibilities to the federal government. It seemed that the only way or the best way at least for the two levels of government to co-operate was through the program of shared services. This legislation is a transitional measure. It is felt by the government, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, that the time has come when these shared programs can be discontinued without harm to the economy of the country. I would not agree entirely with this, but this is the contention and these opinions are honestly held. We are all working for the good of the country. We are working for national unity and we are working for a strong and united Canada. The government has taken the stand that in order to promote unity and good feeling in the country these shared programs should now be discontinued in any province that wishes to discontinue them. It is of a transitional nature. It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), by the minister and others, that these programs can now safely be discontinued and that national unity may be strengthened by a provincial conference consideration of the whole matter of federal-provincial relationships.
Now, what I find it very difficult to understand is why the government could not have waited for a federal-provincial conference to give consideration to this matter and to make a report before taking action to discontinue the shared programs. I can only reach one conclusion, and that is that the reasons for recommending the discontinuance of these programs are not necessarily the reasons which the government have offered. I feel we have to look farther afield for the reasons, and the reasons are not essentially economic; they are social in effect. We have been told often enough that Quebec has been dissatisfied and wishes to assume a greater share of responsibility for their own affairs.

Dominion-Provincial Relations It appears that the government, in their wisdom are offering to the provinces, particularly to the benefit of Quebec, this opportunity to opt out of all the shared programs.
There are many people in this country who view this trend with considerable alarm. There are two schools of thought in this country as to how national unity can best be promoted. One school of thought contends it can be promoted through a strong central government, through what has been called the one Canada concept. I do not know that that term is too accurate as a term, any more than the term opting out is too accurate as a term. There can be plenty of argument over the semantics. However, these terms do have meaning. Opting out has a meaning, and one Canada has a meaning.
Now, we come to another concept and that is the concept of an associate state. The two schools of thought are both concerned with the promotion of national unity but are divided between the one Canada concept and the associate state concept. There are many people who feel that the offer of the federal government to permit the provinces to opt out of these shared programs is tending toward the development of associate states. They fear this concept. They fear that if the provinces each go their own way, that in the end the provinces will become divided.
I am not depending entirely on my own reasoning in dealing with this concept of associate states. I have a Canadian Press report, printed in the London Free Press of March 10, 1965, emanating from Montreal which states:
A system of associated states has been suggested by 40 classical colleges in Quebec province as the solution to Canada's constitutional problems.
There you have one reference to it.
Officials of 29 such colleges said independence for Quebec could come in the future.
Now, that is one of the fears of the people of this country, that the concept of associate states is opening up a door which could eventually lead to a weakening of our central government and a breaking down of the unity of our nation.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am contending that the opting out legislation does

contribute or tend towards this concept of associate states. If we do not view this opting out legislation as part of a general package deal, it makes very little sense. In dealing with this point I should like to look back at the speech by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who has a trained legal mind, just as I believe my friend across the aisle has. This is the way the hon. member for Edmonton West put it, and I am arguing at this point that if we do not consider this opting out legislation as part of a trend or a move in a certain direction, it makes very little sense. This is what he says, as recorded at page 12486 of Hansard:
With the greatest respect, Mr. Speaker, I think this is one of the biggest hoaxes perpetrated on the Canadian public in the last few years.
There is no opting out in this bill. Provinces are going to be given the right to sign supplementary agreements to joint programs in which they are now involved, but those supplementary agreements so far as the great majority of and the most important joint programs covered by the bill are concerned, will not give a province one more iota of freedom or room to manoeuvre. Essentially they will be the same programs, with the one basic exception that provinces will take over their administration.
I believe that has been pointed out adequately by several speakers. This proposed Bill No. C-142 does not change a thing. It permits the provinces who wish to do so- and so far only the province of Quebec has expressed any interest in opting out-a greater measure of autonomy. When you couple the opting out legislation with the stand taken by the federation of classical colleges of Quebec the whole matter becomes clearer. It becomes a picture, a trend, a package deal.
I now come to another report by Canadian Press from Montreal, dealing with a brief submitted by the St. Jean Baptiste Society of Montreal to the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. To be fair, there were some comments in the press to the effect that the society members were not unanimous on this, but the report reads as follows:
Based on the society's oft-expressed view that Quebec should be given the status of an associate state within confederation, the blueprint came complete with a whole new set of federal institutions to carry out limited assignments mutually agreed on by the two "sovereign" states of Quebec and English Canada.
There we have it again.
The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) had this to say in Winnipeg also as reported by Canadian Press:
Quebec-and perhaps other provinces-will have complete autonomy within 10 years. Mr. Caouette

said Quebec demands control of its own credit; permission to develop its natural resources without federal interference; control of its own exports and imports; control over its own immigration; and control of its tax system.
These statements indicate a direction in which the people of Quebec wish to go, and when we look at this opting out legislation in connection with the whole matter of future constitutional relationships we get a picture which is seriously disturbing to many of the people of Canada. Opinions differ with regard to the matter of national unity and the means by which it can be reached, but these views are honestly held. The only way to thresh these matters out and reach reasonable agreement is to express such views freely and honestly in this chamber so that the people may know whether their aspirations and desires are being adequately represented.
In the few minutes left to me I would like to put on the record what Senator Flynn, a senator from Quebec, had to say in the other house, speaking on July 27 in connection with student loans:
Now I feel that this possibility of option offered for all practical purposes to the province of Quebec alone encourages the isolation of that province at a time when it is already encouraged by other circumstances, and this at the expense of Canadian unity. I feel that this optional system is a bad thing.
He had another comment to make in connection with the effect of the federal-provincial conference out of which this legislation grew, and he said this about federal-provincial conferences, and the need for some authority to rule whether legislation comes under provincial or federal jurisdiction:
If we agree on the supreme court, let the legislation be submitted to the supreme court. I object to the constitution being amended by a majority of the provinces.
Suppose this act was ultra vires with regard to the powers of this parliament. Would the fact that nine provinces out of ten agree with the central government make it constitutional? Of course not. However, that is what is happening in the way the government is acting.
With all respect, Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious matter and I do not think the present minority government has any right to proceed with the processing of this legislation without a further mandate from the people of Canada to do so. We did not have this as an issue in the last election, and I do not think the government has the support which it thinks it has among the people of Canada to promote such opting out legislation. I repeat it should not proceed further without a definite mandate from the electors of Canada.

maintopic: INDUSTRY-STUDY OF U.S. ENCROACHMENT OF CANADIAN ECONOMY
INDUSTRY-STUDY OF U.S. ENCROACHMENT OF CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the question period today I indicated my concern at the fact that our law seems so inadequate as to prevent the taking over of Canadian industries by United States control. What brought the matter to my attention most recently was the ruling by the United States department of justice prohibiting Molson breweries from taking over the Hamm brewery, one of the smaller breweries in California. I have been perturbed on this point of take-overs, of the gradual erosion of our industries and our manufacturers by our friends across the border.
I have expressed the opinion previously in this house that it was alarming that in 1962 over $400 million worth of Canadian industry passed forever out of the control of Canadian hands into those of Americans and other foreign investors. But my fears were somewhat allayed by the fact that in 1963, thanks to the measures taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) or at least to the indication by him that he took a dim view of these proceedings, this $400 million worth of take-over was reduced to approximately $50 million worth. My fears were also allayed by the realization that perhaps in time Canadian industry would reverse the trend or look favourably upon the take-over of U.S. industries when opportunities existed.
But what has happened to Molson breweries, in a straightforward attempt to expand

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion their interests in the United States, indicates to us that the Americans are not quite as naive as we Canadians. They have taken adequate protection through the medium of their legislation, including anti-trust laws, to prevent the day when foreign interests, and we are included in that definition, can take over U.S. enterprises without very strong opposition on the part of U.S. industry.
I think the time has come for us to take a second look at those American companies that are already established in Canada and see if they are in effect working as good Canadians. Some of those who have established these rights in our nation should be required by legislation to put up 25 per cent of their stock to be bought by Canadian investors. In other words, it is time they stopped paying lip service to the principle of being Canadian, and did something tangible about it.
Mr. Speaker, I would refer to the Montreal Gazette of Saturday, March 20, and the section known as "Business News". The headline says, "Deal Off... Molson Licks Its Wounds". In this article by Mr. R. G. Gibbens certain things can be read between the lines, if you take the trouble to read it. For instance it says, referring to the justice department of the United States, that it is "a somewhat sphinx-like creatures of modern government". Then it says:
One dictionary describes a Sphinx as "a fabulous monster... supposed to devour all who were unable to answer its riddles..."
"Justice" may hardly be a monster; but the Molson emissaries in Washington never really found the answers to its riddles.
They weren't devoured.. .but they have been licking their wounds ever since the first week in March and it was clear the merger deal would be killed on anti-trust grounds, however vague.
The Molson people listened long and hard for many hours to justice department officials and their position, but they never managed to make sense of the "undue domination" argument. Specific marketing areas in the minds of the justice department were never sharply delineated-but it was clear the key market area of the U.S. at issue was the west-California.
So, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully suggest to the Minister of Finance through the medium of my question today, which will appear in written form tomorrow, that it is high time he and other officials of the government took a second look at the legislation that exists to see if something cannot be done to strengthen it and prevent further take-overs of our Canadian industry by American interests. Certainly if the Americans have had the foresight to write into their anti-trust laws and all the other legislation of that great nation steps to prevent the eventual take-over of their in-

dustries, it is high time that we in our nation, with the gradual erosion going on not only in the field of industry but in communications and culture, stood up and started telling the world that we are Canadians.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INDUSTRY-STUDY OF U.S. ENCROACHMENT OF CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who believes it is not in Canada's best interests for so much of our industry to be under foreign control. We all know-and based on the pressures I have been subjected to in the last two years, perhaps I know better than most people-that this is a very controversial subject. I had hoped that Canadian feelings about this might be relieved if, in addition to the enactment of appropriate laws in Canada, some of our companies were permitted to expand in the United States. The Molson company planned to do this. I was informed of their plans and welcomed them. So I was sorry to learn of the decision of the United States department of justice which will prevent the merger of the Molson and Hamm companies I am afraid some Canadians will conclude that what is good for the gander is not necessarily good for the goose. In answer to my hon. friend's question, let me say we have been giving a great deal of consideration to the kind of legislation that is needed to slow down and eventually to reverse the take-over of Canadian businesses and Canadian resources.
It has been suggested that we should begin with legislation in respect of certain industries-the banks for example. It has been suggested that we should push forward with new investment capital machinery which will place Canadians in a position to compete on equal terms with foreign financial interests. I am thinking of course of the Canada Development Corporation.
In view of the Molson case it has been suggested that we should take a new look at our own anti-combines or anti-trust legislation. I can assure my hon. friend that the government is giving very careful consideration to these and a variety of other proposals and suggestions.

maintopic: CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP-AMENDMENT OF ACT TO ENSURE RELIGIOUS FREEDOM
CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP-AMENDMENT OF ACT TO ENSURE RELIGIOUS FREEDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently a judgment was handed down by the supreme court of Ontario in the Bergsma case which is straightforward in its defiance of human liberties. My question today was a twofold question

and I shall have to deal with it in two parts for that reason.
The first part of my question was whether the government was considering paying the legal fees involved in the appeal that the Bergsmas have made, and will have to be making in the future. The reason for my question is that the Bergsmas, I feel, have attempted to adopt a principle and to fight for something they genuinely believe in themselves, rather than to be hypocritical or even to lie and take a path that they do not mean, which has obviously been the case with thousands of immigrants in Canada who are neither Christian nor Jewish and who would have to use the words "so help me God". Because "God" is a word which is Judaic-Christian in its origin, and therefore Christian in its meaning, and people of other religious beliefs than Christianity and Judaism would have to be hypocritical in taking this oath. Therefore the Bergsmas, if their appeal goes through, would establish a precedent, and I feel that bearing the brunt of the expense of establishing this precedent in accordance with their own principles should be backed financially by the government.
The second part of my question was whether the government is going to do anything about amending the oath of allegiance so that this will not happen in the future. If this had been done in the case of the Bergsmas they would not have had to proceed any further.
In this regard I should like to refer first of all to the citizenship act, section 12 thereof being as follows:
A certificate of citizenship granted to any person under this part.. .shall not take effect until the applicant has taken the oath of allegiance set forth in the second schedule-
On page 20 of the act is found the second schedule which outlines the oath of which I spoke before, the oath of allegiance, ending with the words "so help me God". There is no alternative to this wording, as there is in some other oaths which we take. In the oath of allegiance there is no alternative choice of words.
In the act respecting oaths of allegiance, which is chapter 197 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, section 1 says:
Every person in Canada who.. .in obedience to the directions of any act or law in force in Canada, except the British North America Act, 1867, and the Canadian Citizenship Act, desires to take an oath of allegiance, shall have administered to him and take the oath in the following form and no other:-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
And then the oath to which I have just referred is set out, ending with the words "so help me God".
In the Canadian Bill of Rights, section 1 states:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada-
It does not say a citizen of Canada, but in Canada.
-there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights-
And so on. It seems to me that when I asked the question in the house at the time the Bergsma case was first brought up in the house, I asked whether the bill of rights applied only to people who had obtained their citizenship certificate, and the answer I was given was yes. Yet the bill of rights clearly points out that any person in Canada is entitled to this freedom. Surely we are not going to construe the words "freedom of religion" as meaning only people who have a belief in religion, because surely the freedom of no religion is the same thing as the freedom of religion.
Before I came to the house tonight I obtained a copy of a letter which was sent to the leader of our party, written by a man in Toronto. He states that he wants strongly to protest the existence of that part of the citizenship act which prevents atheists from becoming citizens of this country. Later on he says that we should not discriminate against atheists any more than we should discriminate against any other minority group, such as Negroes and orientals. He also states that as an atheist himself who was born in this country he does not feel that he should be allowed to remain a citizen if immigrants who are also atheists cannot become citizens.
On the strength of this letter, and on the basis of the precedent which has been established, my question is twofold to the government. Will the government consider paying the legal fees of the Bergsma family, and is there any chance of the government amending the citizenship act in such a way that the oath of allegiance will be enlarged to contain an affirmation, rather than just being an oath of allegiance?

maintopic: HIGHWAYS-BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
HIGHWAYS-BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I tried to put a question to the Minister of Public Works. I wanted to know whether he had received from the minister of transport of British Columbia a letter asking for the assistance of the federal government to widen from two to four lanes a section of road between Victoria and Swartz Bay.

Since this house in its wisdom, Mr. Speaker, has not yet seen fit to abolish capital punishment, I think it would be wise for me to continue my remarks in English.
This will be an expensive stretch of highway. It will cost $9J million for 18 miles. But this should come as no surprise to the

federal government. Things in British Columbia are often a little more expensive, a little better or a little bigger than in other parts of Canada. In fact I find that the dominion government was warned of this some time before British Columbia entered confederation, because in looking through the sessional papers for 1870 I noticed a letter from Governor Musgrave of British Columbia to the Governor General of Canada in which he refers to the white inhabitants of British Columbia as being "chiefly male adults of wasteful and expensive habits".

maintopic: HIGHWAYS-BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: All Liberals, I take it.

maintopic: HIGHWAYS-BRITISH COLUMBIA-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Nowadays British Columbians travel a great deal, and the most important highway along which they travel in my area is the one referred to in the letter of the British Columbia minister of highways. Although it is not a part of the trans-Canada highway system, it was built in large measure with federal government assistance over 10 years ago. The federal government of that day recognized the federal responsibility for a highway which connects the capital city of British Columbia with the B.C. mainland by the shortest land route, and passes Victoria's only airport and the federal docks at Sidney.
The two lane highway which was adequate 10 years ago is now outdated. Travellers proceeding today from beautiful and Liberal Victoria to beautiful and largely Liberal Vancouver need nothing more than a good four lane highway to carry them speedily and safely through the also beautiful but politically insecure riding of my hon. friend from Esquimalt-Saanich. I know that if he were in the house he would support me in this request.
What we are asking for is nothing less than a good two lane, bicultural highway going north from Victoria to Swartz Bay and beside it a good, bilingual, two lane highway heading south. I trust that the federal government, lending its aid once again, will make both of these things possible.

I thank you.
